records.name: Idaho
records.summary:
Idaho carries the country's strictest criminalised restroom regime. Its 2026 facility-use law, effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room not matching their birth sex — in government buildings and in any private business open to the public, including gas stations, restaurants and hospitals — with a misdemeanour of up to one year and a felony of up to five years on a repeat within five years. Four successive legislative rounds ran from 2023 to 2026, alongside a ban on official recognition of Pride flags.

A federal lawsuit followed the law's passage; contemporaneous reporting states the law was partially blocked, leaving it in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists. Since then a March 2026 bill extending felony restroom penalties to all public accommodations has passed the House, a March 2026 forced-outting statute has been signed, a birth-marker freeze has been in effect since January 2026, and the federation's Supreme Court declined in 2024 to review the state's bar on gender-affirming care.

freshness.fact: Claim understated, not stale: March 2026 felony bathroom bill (any public accommodation) passed House; March 2026 forced-outting law; Jan 2026 birth-marker freeze in effect; 2024 SCOTUS care-ban denial stands.

records.name: Louisiana
records.summary:
Louisiana posts the country's highest measured killing rate against trans women: 24.7 per 100k trans women per year reported, 11.6 recorded, on the TGEU trans-murder-monitoring base (428 US victims, 2008–2025) — a floor rather than a total, though the same analysis cautions that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, and the top-ranked state records 23.5. In custody, a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence was killed by other inmates at Angola prison on 2 April 2024, at least the 16th violent death of a trans or gender-expansive person that year; killings continued into 2026.

On 31 May 2026 a mob of about ten beat a trans couple, Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders, outside a women's restroom at a park in Benton; no attacker was arrested, while both victims were charged with disturbing the peace and Rush was jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a female marker on her licence. On 15 July 2026 the Bossier Parish Police Jury unanimously approved — on the first of two required votes, reportedly at the sheriff's request — a local ordinance criminalising trans restroom use, described as one of the most punitive in the country. Louisiana has no statewide adult bathroom ban, so the parish ordinance is the state's sharpest instrument.

records.name: Texas
records.summary:
Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.

records.name: Tennessee
records.summary:
Tennessee is the only US state with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere children could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable: the Sixth Circuit revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so its constitutionality has never been decided on the merits; no prosecutions are publicly reported, but a civil-rights suit over a district attorney's threat to charge a 2023 Pride event remains ongoing, and a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure rather than a dead-letter law.

Since 2026 the state has also mandated birth-sex placement in prisons and shelters, and its ban on gender-affirming care for minors was constitutionally upheld by the Supreme Court in June 2025. Killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.

freshness.fact: Drag-act SCOTUS litigation upheld the law; 2025-06-18 Skrmetti upheld minor-care ban; 2026 'Riley Gaines Act' adds birth-sex placement in prisons (and shelter ban) - facility claims current and expanding.

records.name: Kansas
records.summary:
Kansas's SB 244 (signed February 2026) is among the harshest instruments a traveller can meet: it confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings, voids Kansas-issued IDs with corrected markers (licences invalid from 26 February 2026, no grace period, holders notified), and creates a private right of action under which anyone may sue a person they suspect of a violation for about $1,000 — a bounty-style exposure that the February 2026 legal-risk assessment singled out as the cycle's first 'Do Not Travel' addition, warning it 'could meaningfully affect interstate travel'.

Two trans men sued within days of enactment (Doe v. State of Kansas, with civil-liberties counsel), citing fear of violence under the law; a May 2026 injunction covers only the healthcare provisions, leaving the facility and ID regime in force.

freshness.fact: SB244 broad bathroom/ID law in force (no enforcement mechanism per page); Feb 2026 $1,000 bounty signed; the cited Feb-2026 ACLU lawsuit is itself current; May 2026 injunction covers care provisions only.

evidence.title: Kansas Reflector: trans men sue over SB244

records.name: Mississippi
records.summary:
Mississippi enacted public-facility bans in 2024 and 2025 and defines legal sex by birth in statute, placing it in the worst-law group of the July 2026 per-state legal-risk grading.

One institutional counterweight is documented: a federal court sentenced the killer of a trans woman in Lucedale to 49 years for a bias-motivated murder — evidence that violence here can meet real prosecutorial response even while hostile law stands.

records.name: Oklahoma
records.summary:
Oklahoma enacted facility bans in 2022 and 2025 and defines legal sex by birth in statute.

The July 2026 per-state legal-risk assessment lists it among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults.

records.name: Alabama
records.summary:
Alabama's facility bans (2022 and 2024) and its 'Don't Say Gay' law — which extends bathroom restrictions to college campuses — place it in the worst-law group of the July 2026 per-state legal-risk grading.

The 2022–23 school-facility and expression restrictions remain in force with no repeal or adverse 2026 ruling found. Recorded killings of trans women stand at 3.8 per 100k trans women per year.

freshness.fact: 2022-2023 restrictions (school bathroom law HB322-era, 'Don't Say Gay' + facility bill signed) remain in force; no repeal or adverse 2026 ruling found on state page.
